objects.label: Audit
objects.purpose: Tracks AgvId, current Geek task ID, and command GUID from robotics; changes audited in Audits.
objects.when_to_use: Corroborate robotics command GUID ↔ Geek task ID mapping during stuck command / resend investigations.
objects.not_for: Primary AGV active-error triage (use Robotics SystemActiveError / AgvActiveError).

objects.label: GeekAgv
objects.purpose: Geek+ task history and lattice code ↔ station ID mapping.
objects.when_to_use: Confirm Geek task history or lattice/station translation for roster / command issues.
objects.not_for: Live AGV active error list (Robotics AgvActiveError / SystemActiveError).

objects.label: OPCComms
objects.purpose: OPC connection parameters and startup-subscribed tags for tipper/hospital PLC communication.
objects.when_to_use: When diagnosing tipper/hospital tag subscription or OPC configuration (with Ignition OPC Connections).
objects.not_for: Gateway performance / memory crash root-cause alone (use Ignition gateway UI + Event Viewer).

objects.label: Robotics
objects.purpose: AGV state machine DB: locations, robots, commands/tasks, charging, hospital, dwell, AGV/system errors, system status.
objects.when_to_use: L2/L3 read-only SSMS for fleet roster, active errors, dwell, shutdown staging, robot commands/tasks, sort lifecycle status.
objects.not_for: Mutating recovery (use APIs/Apidog); physical E-stop clear (operator only).

objects.label: SorterSweeper
objects.purpose: Tote state machine DB: locations/lanes, tippers/tags, items/scans, totes/exchanges/bag-out, ESTOP, sort/system state, tasks.
objects.when_to_use: Lane/chute, tipper faults, missing dims / scan path, tote lifecycle/exchange, bag-out, ESTOP callbacks, sort GUID metrics.
objects.not_for: Geek RMS map-only triage without corroboration; physical tipper LOTO (operator).

objects.label: EntityLogs
objects.purpose: OptiSweep code logging (DeveloperLogs); WCS default DB OptiSweep uses for logging.
objects.when_to_use: Debug which code path / line produced an error during L2/L3 investigation.
objects.not_for: Primary operational state of AGVs/totes (use Robotics / SorterSweeper).

objects.label: WcsError
objects.purpose: Adjacency/corroboration path; confirm site presence at ingest.

Operator Stats Response Time Metrics: The Operator Stats section provides three metrics for each tipper: Resp Time Max (ms), Resp Time Min (ms), and Resp Time Avg (ms). The response time is measured from when the tote is gripped by the tipper to when the operator presses the button to initiate tipping. A DATA RESET button is available to zero all data.

Sorter Tote Replacement Rule: It is essential that a tote manually removed from the sorter stand is returned to its original position with the same Tote ID. Failure to do so will require rescanning to properly associate the tote with its designated location.

Bulk sort and bag-out functions: During the bulk of the sort, items are actively sorted and AGVs take full totes to the tippers for bagging. The bag-out cycle is described as cycling all locations that still have any items in a tote so the sort can be finished out.

Parcel lifecycle into the sorter: Before parcels reach the OptiSweep-controlled portion of the system, they are unloaded from trailers in bulk onto a series of belts that lead to sorter induction. As parcels move through this flow, system messaging is triggered and parcel data becomes available.

Parcel lifecycle messaging before and at sorter induction: Before parcels reach the system, they are unloaded from trailers in bulk onto belts that lead to sorter induction. The slide states that the first Chat message includes a tracking ID, dimensions, and package type.

Potential destination as a sortable destination set: The speaker explains that UPS may provide multiple possible destinations for an order. In the example discussed, a system can have many sortable destinations and a parcel may be eligible for one of several of them.

ZIP code to destination mapping is handled upstream: According to the speaker, a parcel has a ZIP code, and UPS internally maintains a mapping file where a ZIP code can map to a single destination or multiple destinations. The transcript also states that this is dynamic and comes from the ASX system.

Sort confirmation or divert confirm message as critical tracking input: The transcript explains that after a parcel is sorted, the next message from chat indicates a divert confirm or sort confirmation. This message is described as critical. If it is not received or processed, the system does not have a record of where the parcel went and may not know what is in the tote.

Dependence on dimension and weight data rather than chute sensors: The transcript explicitly states that there are no photo eyes or sensors at the chute and that fullness-related calculations use weight and dimensions. It also notes that weight is part of the dimension data received, and that weight sensors are not present on the robots for this purpose.

Exchange staging thresholds for tote fullness: The segment explicitly mentions thresholds related to the exchange process. It states that staging for an exchange can happen when a tote is immediately full, completely full, or imminently filled. The OCR text also supports the concept that staging can happen when a tote is imminently full or completely full.

AGV zone designation and under-rack lift positioning: According to the segment, an AGV with no tote that is designated to the tote zone moves under the racking to position for a lift. The tote is then lifted in position. The speaker emphasizes that an AGV runs under the racks of the totes and lifts up a tote.

Post-exchange AGV role transition: After the AGV with the empty tote moves into the rack location and lowers its tote, the segment explains that this AGV then becomes the AGV that will pick up the next tote. The OCR text similarly states that the AGV with no tote becomes the AGV that will pick up the next full tote in that zone.

Chute opening timing and KPI emphasis: The speaker states that the chute is opened when the AGV moves in, not when it drops a tote. This behavior is described as intentional and tied to strict KPI requirements and the need to speed up exchanges.

Chute closure behavior and exchange timing targets: The speaker states that the chute gets closed when the chute is full, and discusses the effect of not keeping up with exchanges or not tipping quickly enough. In that condition, chutes will eventually close because everything gets full.

Shutdown queue locations and tote-dependent shutdown positioning: The segment explains that shutdown queues exist in the sorter layout. It states that some shutdown locations are under the rack and that AGVs move to shutdown locations during shutdown. The narration distinguishes locations for AGVs without totes and a location for AGVs with totes.

Sort phases require transitions between runs: The speaker explains that operations may include multiple sorts in a day, such as preload, day sort, and twilight. These sorts do not simply run into each other because they serve different purposes and route volume differently.

Sorter zones constrain AGV pickup and drop-off areas: The segment states that the sorter side has zones and compares them to work areas on the manual side. An AGV in a zone only picks up and drops off within that zone. The speaker describes AGV behavior as coming into its zone, checking whether anything needs to be exchanged, and then moving on.

Shutdown-state AGV replacement behavior through hospital: The speaker gives a specific shutdown-state scenario: if an AGV that does not have a tote is removed and another AGV is added, the added AGV goes through the hospital first. The transcript then states it determines that an AGV is missing and goes to the shorter side.

Charger module queue and tote handling: The transcript explains that the charger has an entrance queue and tote locations where an AGV drops off its tote while it goes to charge. The speaker states that it does not like to charge with totes on it.

Shutdown queues hold AGVs in shutdown state: The speaker explains that shutdown queues are where AGVs remain while shut down. During startup, AGVs move from shutdown queues into their own zones. The segment notes a four-zone example and says AGVs with totes return and get ready.

Special locations can represent different operational functions: The presenter states that to UPS, a special location could be a sort location and could also be a tipper location. The source emphasizes that the underlying system does not inherently distinguish these two special locations; the distinction comes from how the site uses the location and represents it in its state...

Charger IDs as unique charger identifiers: The presenter states that charger IDs exist similarly to station IDs. Clicking the relevant icon shows all chargers in the system with their unique IDs. An example is given that if the system has 10 chargers, there will be 10 unique charger IDs.

Task persistence across restart versus removal: The speaker states that if the robot is in the middle of a transaction, it will resume the transaction after restart, and that the task does not get lost for restarts if the robot does not get lost.

WCS reinitialization depends on tote connectivity and binding state: According to the transcript, WCS needs the AGV to lose connectivity with the tote in order to reinitialize that AGV. If the AGV is removed and added back, it may still be considered bound to the tote, but not with a proper binding.

Layer Count reflects single-density rack configuration: The speaker explains that all shelves or racks are single density and only have one layer. The Layer Count shown on the screen is therefore tied to the rack property setup and is expected to be one for this environment.

Logic ID field is present but not used in this environment: During the walkthrough of the screen fields, the speaker identifies Logic ID, Layer Count, and another count-related field. The speaker then states that they do not use the Logic ID in this environment.

Exception box and related fields are available but not used: A trainee asks about abnormal use, abnormal code location, code location, and the exception box shown on the right side of the screen. The response states that these are features they have not had to use and are part of other Geek Plus capabilities.

Station labels are distinct from tote indicators and have associated IDs: The speaker explains that containers without the blue or dark blue indicators at the bottom may physically look like a label, but they are special labels with additional properties. These are identified as stations, and the training states that the stations have IDs associated with them.

Location number lookup for tote, rack, or AGV association: OCR text states that a tote can be found by typing the location number and selecting the rack or AGV it is located on if it is in the system. This describes a lookup capability available from the displayed screen.

Orange station cells include workstation ID information: The source states that if a cell code is a special cell, it is a station. Orange cells represent stations. When an orange cell is selected, the displayed information includes an additional field identified as the workstation ID. An example is given where the station ID is 862.

Cell code is a unique physical QR code identifier: During the discussion, the speaker clarifies that the displayed value is not an array with multiple values and is not a route ID. Instead, it is a unique cell code and a physical QR code number. The source explicitly states that a cell can only have one cell code.

Load and unload direction fields describe tote-dependent travel permissions between cells: The source explains that if only unload direction is activated between two cells, only AGVs without a tote can travel there. If only loaded direction is activated between two cells, only AGVs with a tote can go between those cells, and AGVs without a tote cannot.

AGB HV charge percentage shown in the power section: The transcript states that if the AGB is selected, there is a small section labeled power that shows the charge percentage of the HV battery. An example value of 50% is mentioned.

Low HV charge is an operational concern during extended delays: The speaker describes a case where an AGB sat for hours waiting to be tipped on a tipper and then died. The transcript also notes that if an AGB is already around 30% to 32% charge and it takes one or two hours to fix an issue, the situation moves closer to a problematic battery state.

Low-battery thresholds affecting task acceptance and startup: According to the speaker, under 20% battery the robot will not accept any new task. At 15% battery it will turn off automatically and cannot be turned on until it is moved to a charger. The discussion emphasizes avoiding operation near 15% and treating 20% as a practical lower boundary for continued use.

Low-battery robots can regain enough charge for system re-entry after a short charging period: The speakers state that after reaching a low state, it may take about 10 minutes to get enough charge to be able to start and add the robot back into the system. An example is also given that a robot at 25% charged for 15 minutes may reach about 40%, which is described as sufficient for the system to cycle it on its...

Charger availability matters more at sites with limited charger count: The speakers mention a site example with only two chargers and warn that if one charger is left off or not re-enabled, the system effectively operates with only one charger, increasing charging delays. This is contrasted with larger sites where the impact may be less significant.

Hot bin behavior in OptiSweep: The source states that hot bins will trigger all totes marked as hot bin to close chute and exchange. The transcript also explains hot bins as the highest priority bins, associated with items that need to get out quickly, such as for a trailer departure.

Indicator message reference for hot bin marking: The transcript states that a message is sent saying what is hopped in, and that the message type is literally called the indicator. Items with that indicator are then exchanged. This establishes indicator as a named message reference associated with hot bin or hop in marking in this training segment.

System Shutdown state for AGV charger rotation: The OCR text states: 'When the sort is done the system should be put in a shutdown state for AGVs to rotate on the charger.' This places System Shutdown in the context of post-sort AGV charging management on the Overall System Aveva API page.

Metrics and errors pop-up references: The transcript says 'get metrics gets all the system metrics, pops it up' and 'Get errors is a pop up as well.' The OCR text labels these items as 'Get metrics' and 'Get errors' and describes them as opening the metrics page and current errors respectively.

Station ID is used as the tote destination reference: The speaker says that when an AGV or tote is removed from the sorter, a station ID can be specified so the tote can be associated with a destination station. In response to a question about how the station is known, the speaker says it is in RMS and that when a cell is picked the station ID can be seen.

Item exchange KPI fields shown on the System Metrics page: The transcript and OCR identify the KPI fields shown on the page: Average Item Count Per Exchange, Median System Generated Exchange in seconds, Last System Generated Exchange, Number of Exchanges, Number of HotBins, Number of MissSorts, Number of SurePost, Percent of Exchanges, Status, and Zone.

Zone information displayed alongside KPI data: The transcript explains that the page shows what zone is associated with the displayed information. It also states that every side has multiple zones, with an example comparison of one side having 7 zones and another having 4.

AGV-related limitation for tote initialization: The transcript states that if the totes are on an AGV, the system response can say the tote cannot be initialized. It also mentions that only AGVs not in the system or AGVs that have been removed are eligible in that context, and that a new tote not previously seen or a removed tote may be handled differently.

Volume statistics categories: The OCR text explicitly lists 'Volume (Total Exchanges, To Tipper, To Hospital).' The transcript similarly references 'volume, number of exchanges to tipper to hospital.' This indicates that the statistics view includes volume-related metrics broken out by total exchanges and destination-oriented categories.

Customer-requested origin of custom metrics: In the transcript, the speaker says the custom defined metrics are 'stuff that UPS requested and worked out with our team.' This provides operational context that these metrics are not presented as generic platform defaults in this segment, but as customer-requested calculations developed collaboratively.

Metrics are scoped to sort GUID and reset each sort: The presenter explains that when the system cycles sort, it sends a reset metrics bit. Todd picks up that signal and resets the Tipper metrics, and a webhook/API flow generates a new sort GUID.

UPS sorter data and tote destination concepts: The source identifies scan tunnel data as including parcel dimensions and load category. Sort information is sent from XLE, possible destinations are collected for each parcel, and sort confirmation is sent from the sorter.

Audit and Geek AGV task logging: The Audit database tracks the AGDID, current Geek task ID, and command GUID sent by the robotics engine. Changes to the relevant table are tracked in an audits table. The Geek AGV database contains an action-logging model that logs tasks to Geek Plus and serves as a history of tasks.

Lattice codes and station identifiers: The lattice code model stores lattice codes and their respective station IDs. When a tote is inducted or dropped off, Geek requires a lattice code for the location. The Geek COM module uses the table to convert a station ID from robotics module requests to the corresponding lattice code.

Location types and location status terminology: The listed location types include sorter entrance queue, sorter queue, sorter exit queue, tipper, tipper queue, tipper exit queue, hospital drop-off, hospital entrance queue, hospital pickup, hospital exit, queue shutdown, off-the-end shutdown queue, GLD pre-queue, and GLD pre-queue exit.

Sorter-side tipper distribution concept: A sorter side is described as being associated with a group of tippers. The transcript explains that tipper count can represent the closest four tippers and that assignment uses another mapping.

Location zones, cell codes, and coordinates: Zones are described as a system concept used on the sorter side, with the transcript referring to seven zones in the example shown. Cell codes are compared with RMS node codes and are described as terminology intended to remain modular across vendors.

Sort locations database model: The sort locations database model contains sorted locations and their respective queue locations. Queue locations are positioned behind sorted locations and are used by AGVs with an empty tote to fill a location when an exchange occurs.

Shutdown staging database model: The shutdown staging table maps where AGVs are staged during a shutdown state. The training describes separate staging concepts for AGVs with totes and AGVs without totes.

Sorter queue and array sequence concept: The discussion refers to a sorter zone exit queue sequence ID and notes that the collection may also be considered an array. The terminology is treated as interchangeable for describing the ordered set of AGVs associated with sorter zones.

Charging database model tables: The charging database model includes a charging area table, a charging location table, and a charging threshold table. Together, these tables represent charging-area boundaries, individual charger mappings, tote-stand associations, and charging-related values used by the application.

Charging area configuration: The charging area database model stores charging areas and their entrance IDs and exit IDs. The training describes charging areas as having multiple chargers and includes a disabled indicator for the area.

Charging location and tote-stand mapping: The charging location database model stores each individual charger and the station where it is located. It also records the tote stand associated with the charger, the charging area associated with it, and whether the charger is disabled.

Charging threshold values: The charging threshold database model stores values used in application logic to identify when an AGV needs charging, when it can leave a charger, and when emergency charging is required. The source does not specify the threshold values themselves.

Robot Command Database active-command tracking: The table contains commands while they are active, including command status and timing information. The transcript describes statuses such as sent, in progress, completed, errored, and cancelled. Completed commands are archived to Robot Command Activity.

Robot Command Activity historical records: The historical record includes the command name, command status, robot name, container, station, parameters sent to the Geek Plus COM module, sent time, in-progress time, execution time, station circuit, and total time.

Robot location and queue capacity concepts: The transcript describes current location ID and destination location fields in the robot database model. It also refers to maximum AGV capacity associated with robot locations or queues, including examples where a tipper may allow one or, in some cases, two AGVs.

Robot Task Current and Archived Records: The source describes separate current and archived records: the Robot Task database model contains the current task information, while completed tasks are moved to Robot Task Activity.

AGV Error Reference Model: The AGV Error model is described as a lookup or dictionary of AGV errors. It stores the error code and an associated description. Errors are classified as critical or non-critical for metric purposes. The transcript gives an example in which an error code is associated with a description such as a front bumper trigger.

Location Dwell Current and Archived Records: A dwell record represents how long an AGV has been sitting at a tracked sort location. The Location Active Dwell model contains the current dwell, and once the AGV leaves the location, the dwell information is archived to Location Dwell Activity.

Location Active Dwell Model: The displayed model includes AgvName, Station, and SortGuid fields. Dwell tracking is represented as a true-or-false setting for stations, and the model collects an AGV's active dwell while it remains at a tracked location.

Location Dwell Activity Archive: The archived activity display includes AgvName, Station, SortGuid, Start Time, Finish Time, and Total Time. The source shows completed dwell examples with timestamps and total durations.

Operational Dwell Metrics: Hospital dwell time is described as how long an AGV waits before it can drop off its tote at the hospital. Tipper dwell time is described as how long a tote remains at the tipper before it is tipped. The discussion also references entrance queue and execution-related timing.

System Error Definition table: The displayed Robotics Database table includes system error names, areas, descriptions, and defined resolutions. Examples shown include AgvHasNotMoved30Seconds in the AGV area with the description "AGV has not moved in 30 seconds" and the resolution "Reboot AGV"; AgvOutOfSequence with "AGV is out of sequence"; and...

System Database Model Fields: The database view identifies the fields EntityInserted, EntityLastUpdate, Status, and SortGuid. The displayed record includes an insertion timestamp, a last-update timestamp, status Running, and a GUID value.

Sorter, Lane, and Tipper Database Fields: Visible field names include SorterName, SorterSideName, SorterId, LaneName, LaneStatus, Lane, Tipper, TipperStatus, TipperStation, TipperStationId, TipperLoadType, TipperDeparture, TipperSelect, and related identifiers such as SortGuid and LocationId.

Package, Tote, and Destination Database Fields: The displayed fields include PackageUid, TrackingNumber, Itemid, PackageClassification, OriginalDestination, FinalDestination, Destination, ToteName, ToteId, ToteError, ToteTypeName, ToteNotFound, SortName, SortGuid, TotalSorted, StartTime, FinishTime, and TotalTime.

Sorter database model overview: The sorter model includes storage-oriented data and relationships between database entities. The segment describes the model as an overview comparable to the robotics model and notes that some fields represent configuration or activities.

Sorter interface identifiers: The XLE IP is described as the receiver IP address, and the XLE name is described as the receiver name. Both identifiers are associated with sending messages to the sorter.

Items model and sorter package lifecycle: The system listens to Scan Data 2, sort, and sort-confirm messages from UPS. Items are updated as messages are received and removed when they divert to their final destination. The transcript also refers to recirculation as an item remaining on the sorter.

Scan Data 2 package attributes: The transcript identifies package unique ID, tracking number, length, width and height information, weight, and package classification as data supplied by Scan Data 2. The lane activity information also includes package UID, tracking number, length, width, height, and cube.

Item cube adjustment and default dimension models: The item cube adjustment model stores the percentage of cube to use based on package classification. The transcript describes classifications such as boxes, flats, and poly bags, while noting uncertainty about some classification codes.

Lane activity message and routing fields: The lane activity view shows the message type, including Scan Data 2 and sort confirmation. It can associate packages with auto-induct sources using package ID information. The transcript references auto-induct identifiers such as Auto Induct 1 and Auto Induct 2, which are defined by UPS.

Exchange model and exchange activity archive: When a chute is closed, an active exchange is created in the active exchange model. When an empty tote replaces it, the exchange is closed and archived to exchange activity. The active model retains a smaller set of current exchanges, while the activity model stores historical exchange information.

Bag-out tracking and archive model: When a bag-out closes as requested, open chutes are closed. Totes containing an item are marked for exchange, and an entry is made in active bag out. The bag-out record is archived to bag out activity once the tote has been tipped.

Sort model and reset metrics: When UPS cycles a sort, it calls the Reset Metrics API. This opens closed chutes and creates a new SortName and SortGuid. Activity is logged with sort identifiers for historical, sort-to-sort metrics. The referenced Sorter Sweeper Database screen displays sort names, current sort values, and SortGuid values.

Task model and task activity archive: The task model tracks tasks sent to the robotics engine. The described task data includes task ID, task name, tote ID, station, and task status. Completed tasks are archived to task activity. The training compares this active-versus-archived structure with other OptiSweep models.

Operational data is collected across multiple separate tools: Using separate tools to assemble operational data increases the time required to obtain a complete view. The discussion notes an effort to narrow information collection toward a standard or single place for accessing the information, but does not identify a finalized system or implementation.

Package Measurement and Identification Fields: Visible columns include PackageUid, TrackingNumber, Length, Width, Height, Weight, and Cube. Example rows show numeric values for dimensions, weight, and cube, while some records contain dashes or incomplete-looking values. The source does not establish units, validation rules, or interpretation of missing values.

Sort confirmation filtering: The presenter describes filtering on sort confirmation to inspect records and compare the associated dimension and sort data. The table contains SortConf entries alongside package-level values.

Dimensioner behavior after a power flicker: The segment states that a power flicker caused the dimensioners to not reboot properly and that the dimensioners were rebooted in response. This is presented as an observed equipment behavior associated with power interruption.

Expected dimension data from dimensioners: The discussion says that support expects to receive dimension data and that database review can show when the expected data is not present. The source does not define the complete data flow, timing, or ownership of the dimensioners.

SystemActiveErrorModel table used for active AGV error visibility: The provided SQL statement selects records from [Helix2x_1Prod_Robotics].[dbo].[SystemActiveErrorModel]. In this source, that table is the referenced data component used to retrieve active error information associated with AGV error review.
